rows.label: Occam's razor
rows.description: philosophical principle used to judge credibility of statements
rows.hook: holds that the simplest explanation with the fewest assumptions is usually the best one

rows.label: Three Laws of Robotics
rows.description: set of rules devised by the science fiction author Isaac Asimov
rows.hook: sets rules that a mechanical servant may never harm a human, from a sci-fi story series

rows.label: Goodhart's law
rows.description: adage that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure
rows.hook: warns that once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure

rows.label: Murphy's law
rows.description: an adage or epigram that is typically stated as: "Anything that can go wrong, will go wrong".
rows.hook: claims that anything that can go wrong will go wrong

rows.label: Hanlon's razor
rows.description: philosophical adage stating "Never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity."
rows.hook: advises not to blame malice for what stupidity can adequately explain

rows.label: The Peter Principle
rows.description: book and concept by Laurence J. Peter that states that people in a hierarchy tend to rise to "a level of respective incompetence"
rows.hook: says employees in a hierarchy get promoted until they reach a job they cannot do well

rows.label: Moore's law
rows.description: observation on the growth of integrated circuit capacity
rows.hook: predicts that the number of transistors on a computer chip doubles about every two years

rows.label: Pareto principle
rows.description: statistical principle about ratio of effects to causes
rows.hook: says roughly 80 percent of effects come from 20 percent of causes

rows.label: Conway's law
rows.description: observation that organizations design systems mirroring their communication structures (Melvin Conway, 1968)
rows.hook: says the design of software mirrors the communication structure of the organization that builds it

rows.label: Betteridge's law of headlines
rows.hook: holds that any news story title ending in a question mark can be answered with no

rows.label: Poe's law
rows.description: adage of Internet culture that, without a clear indicator of intent, one can’t parody extreme views such that some can’t mistake it for a sincere expression of the parodied views
rows.hook: notes that extreme views online cannot be parodied without someone mistaking the joke for sincerity

rows.label: Zipf's law
rows.hook: states that the most common word in a language appears about twice as often as the second most common

rows.label: Parkinson's law
rows.description: adage that work expands to fill the time available
rows.hook: says work expands to fill the time available for its completion

rows.label: Benford's law
rows.description: observation about the frequency distribution of leading digits in many real-life sets of numerical data
rows.hook: finds that in many real-world datasets the digit 1 leads far more often than any other digit

rows.label: Clarke's three laws
rows.description: three adages proposed by British science fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke about science and technology
rows.hook: includes the idea that advanced enough technology would look like magic to us
